newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zulu chief says S.African peace moves might falter.
newsitem.headline: Zulu chief says S.African peace moves might falter.

text.p: Zulu chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi has warned that tentative peace moves in South Africa's troubled KwaZulu-Natal province would come to nothing if the killing of his party members continued.

At an annual congress of his Inkatha Freedom Party in Ulundi, the Zulu heart of KwaZulu-Natal, Buthelezi said although he supported peace talks between Inkatha and its fiercest rivals, the African National Congress (ANC), they would become meaningless if violence against Inkatha was not probed.

"I rejoice that these talks are taking place and I congratulate those leaders on both sides who have managed to pacify their communities by building on-the-ground goodwill and reconciliation," he told thousands of party faithfuls this weekend.

"However, I cannot be silent before the failure of the ANC's leadership to take strong and effective action within its ranks to stop the carnage of our people and to investigate the systematic assassination of over 400 of our leaders and office bearers."

Buthelezi said recent political killings in the province were also putting at risk the top-level talks between the two parties aimed at ending more than a decade of bloody feuding which has left some 14,000 people dead.

"This is not encouraging," he said, referring to the killings. "Unless we all join hands to do something about it, our noble KwaZulu-Natal peace initiative will remain no more than just another charade."
The independent violence monitoring group, the Human Rights Committee, said 49 people were killed in June in politically motivated attacks in KwaZulu-Natal, the highest toll since June 1996.
Buthelezi also told delegates the statutory Truth and Reconcilition Commission would create conflict and should be scrapped.
The commission was set up to cleanse and heal the hurt inflicted by all sides during minority white rule.
"It is obvious that the commission has failed in its primary objective to bring about national reconciliation and should be scrapped before the damages inflicted on South Africa become irreparable."

He said the commission, headed by Nobel peace laureate Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was creating the impression the ANC had done no wrong in its decades-long struggle to end minority white rule before coming to power in the first all-race elections in 1994.
"It is quite clear that the truth commission is aimed at portraying the ruling party as knights in shining armour and the rest of us as villains," the Zulu chief told journalists later.
